stages.title: The 12 Principles of Animation
stages.description: The classic Disney principles that make motion read as weighty, clear and alive, whatever the tool.
learningObjectives: Name the 12 principles and where they come from
Explain squash and stretch, anticipation and staging with a concrete example
Explain slow in/slow out, arcs, and follow-through/overlapping action
Distinguish secondary action, timing, exaggeration, solid drawing and appeal

explainBack.question: Animate a bouncing ball and then a character jumping: which of the 12 principles would you apply, and how does each one change the motion?
rubric: The principles come from Disney animators Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas in the 1981 book The Illusion of Life
Squash and stretch conveys weight and flexibility, and the object's volume should stay the same while it squashes or stretches
Anticipation is a preparatory move before the main action (e.g. bending the knees before a jump)
Slow in and slow out means more frames near the start and end of a move so it accelerates and decelerates; natural motion follows arcs
Follow-through and overlapping action: parts of the body keep moving after the character stops and different parts move at different rates

resources.title: 12 Principles of Animation (Official Full Series)
resources.description: Alan Becker's animated walkthrough of all twelve principles, each demonstrated with short stick-figure and object examples.
keyPoints: Covers all 12 principles in one series
Demonstrates each principle with an animated example
Also available as individual per-principle videos in a playlist

resources.title: Twelve basic principles of animation
resources.description: Encyclopedia overview of the twelve principles with their origin and a short explanation and example for each.
keyPoints: Introduced by Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas in The Illusion of Life (1981)
Squash and stretch: volume stays constant while the shape deforms
Anticipation prepares the audience for an action, like bending knees before a jump
Slow in/out adds frames near the ends of a move; most natural motion follows arcs
Follow-through: parts keep moving after the character stops, at different rates

resources.title: The 12 principles of animation
resources.description: Plain-language summary of each principle with everyday examples such as a golfer's backswing and a bouncing ball.
keyPoints: Bouncing ball flattening on impact illustrates squash and stretch
A golfer swinging back first is anticipation
Objects ease in and ease out, accelerating and decelerating like a real person
Heavier objects need more frames to look natural (timing)

stages.title: Timing, Spacing & Frame Rates
stages.description: How the number of frames (timing) and the distance between drawings (spacing) control speed and weight, and how keys, breakdowns and in-betweens are planned.
learningObjectives: Distinguish timing from spacing and explain how each affects perceived speed
Define keys, breakdowns and in-betweens and read a simple timing chart
Explain animating on ones, twos and threes at 24 fps
Compare straight-ahead and pose-to-pose workflows

explainBack.question: Explain the difference between timing and spacing, what keys, breakdowns and in-betweens are, and what it means to animate 'on twos' at 24 fps.
rubric: Spacing is how far the subject moves between drawings: larger gaps read as faster motion, smaller gaps as slower; timing is how many frames an action or pose takes
Keys are the main (start/end) poses; breakdowns are intermediate poses that define how the motion travels; in-betweens fill the remaining frames
At the standard 24 fps, on ones means 24 new drawings per second, on twos 12 (each held two frames), on threes 8
Straight-ahead animates frame 1 onward in order (good for fluid effects like smoke or water); pose-to-pose sets keys first, then fills in between (easier to plan timing for characters)

resources.title: Animation basics: The art of timing and spacing - TED-Ed
resources.description: A short TED-Ed lesson using bouncing balls to show how small frame-to-frame changes in timing and spacing alter the motion.
keyPoints: Uses bouncing balls as the core example
Shows how small frame-to-frame changes alter the feel of motion
Introduces timing and spacing as separate controls

resources.title: Frame by Frame: What Really Happens Between Two Key Poses
resources.description: University article explaining key poses, breakdowns and in-betweens, and how spacing and timing control the feel of motion.
keyPoints: Key frames are the start and end poses of an action
Breakdowns define how motion travels, e.g. a change of direction
Larger shifts between drawings mean faster motion; smaller mean slower
Timing (frames per pose) makes action snappy or smooth
Software can interpolate in-betweens, adjusted via curves

resources.title: Week 3: Animation Fundamentals - Timing and Movement
resources.description: College course notes on straight-ahead vs pose-to-pose, in-betweens, breakdowns and timing charts, applied to a bouncing ball.
keyPoints: Straight ahead starts on frame 1 and proceeds in order; suits smoke or water
Pose to pose sets keys first, then fills transitions; preferred for characters
Fewer in-betweens look choppier/faster; more look smoother/slower
Timing charts mark keys, breakdowns and in-betweens along a line

resources.title: What does animating on ones, twos, and threes mean?
resources.description: Quick guide to holding drawings for one, two or three frames at 24 fps and when each rate is used.
keyPoints: Standard 2D animation runs at 24 frames per second
On ones: 24 new drawings per second, for fast action
On twos: 12 new drawings per second, the most common choice
On threes: 8 per second, often seen in anime; rates can be mixed

resources.title: Tutorial: Animating with Timing and Spacing
resources.description: A professional animator's tutorial on using timing and spacing (and ones, twos, threes) to create weight and stylised rhythm.
keyPoints: Starts from the bouncing ball to show acceleration via spacing
Holding poses and snapping between them creates stylised rhythm
Blocks poses from reference, then refines curves in a graph editor
Experiments with ones, twos and threes for impact

stages.title: Keyframes & the Graph Editor
stages.description: Setting keyframes in Blender and shaping the in-betweens with F-curves, interpolation modes, handles and easing.
learningObjectives: Explain what a keyframe stores and insert/delete keyframes in Blender
Read an F-curve: time on the X axis, property value on the Y axis
Choose between Constant, Linear and Bézier interpolation
Use handle types and easing to shape acceleration

explainBack.question: You keyframed a cube moving from left to right. Describe what a keyframe is, how Blender fills the frames in between, and how you would make the motion snap, move mechanically, or ease in and out.
rubric: A keyframe is a marker in time that stores the value of a property; in the 3D Viewport I inserts a keyframe and Alt-I removes it
Interpolation between keys is shown as F-curves in the Graph Editor, with time (frames) on X and the property value on Y
Constant holds the last key's value (stepped), Linear gives straight segments, Bézier (the default) gives smooth curves
Bézier handle types (e.g. automatic vs free) and the easing mode change the curve's shape; in the Graph Editor T sets interpolation, V sets handle type and Ctrl-E sets easing

resources.title: Beginners Guide to Animation in blender 4 - Part 2 - Graph Editor
resources.description: Beginner-focused walkthrough of Blender's Graph Editor for refining keyframed motion.
keyPoints: Introduces the Graph Editor in Blender 4
Shows editing keyframes as curves
Part of a beginner animation series

resources.title: Keyframes Introduction
resources.description: Defines a keyframe and explains how interpolation between keys is represented by F-curves.
keyPoints: A keyframe is a marker of time that stores a property's value
Interpolation is controlled by F-curves
X axis is time, Y axis is the property value
Object name turns yellow in the viewport on a keyed frame

resources.title: Keyframes: Editing
resources.description: How to insert, delete and auto-record keyframes in Blender.
keyPoints: I in the 3D Viewport opens the Insert Keyframe menu
Alt-I deletes keys on the current frame
Auto Keying records keys whenever transforms change
Detailed editing happens in the Graph Editor and Dope Sheet

resources.title: F-Curves Introduction
resources.description: Explains F-curves, the Constant/Linear/Bézier interpolation modes, handle types and extrapolation.
keyPoints: Constant holds the last key's value, giving a stepped curve
Linear gives straight segments
Bézier is the default and gives smooth curves
Automatic handles keep curves smooth; free handles allow sharp changes
Extrapolation sets behaviour before the first and after the last key

resources.title: F-Curves: Editing
resources.description: Graph Editor operators for changing interpolation, handle type and easing of selected keys.
keyPoints: T sets the interpolation mode of selected keyframes
V sets the handle type
Ctrl-E sets the easing mode

stages.title: 3D Modeling Fundamentals: Meshes, Topology & UVs
stages.description: How a polygon mesh is built from vertices, edges and faces, why quad-based topology matters, and how UV unwrapping maps 2D textures onto 3D surfaces.
learningObjectives: Define vertices, edges and faces and the face types (triangles, quads, n-gons)
Explain edge loops, poles and why quads are preferred for deformation and subdivision
Explain what UV coordinates are and why a mesh needs unwrapping
Describe how seams guide unwrapping and when Smart UV Project fits

explainBack.question: Describe what a 3D mesh is made of, what good topology looks like for a character that will bend, and how you would prepare that mesh to receive an image texture.
rubric: A mesh is made of vertices (points in 3D space), edges (connecting two vertices) and faces (the rendered surface)
Faces are triangles, quads or n-gons (more than four vertices); quads deform well and are preferred for animation and subdivision
Edge loops are continuous rings of edges important for deformation; poles are vertices with 3, 5 or more edges where loops cannot continue
UV mapping assigns each face a place on a flat 2D image (U = left-right, V = up-down) so image textures can be applied
Unwrap flattens the mesh by cutting along marked seams; Smart UV Project cuts automatically by angle and suits mechanical objects or architecture

resources.title: You Can Understand 3D Topology (It's Not As Hard As It Looks)
resources.description: A beginner-friendly explanation of what topology is and why edge flow matters.
keyPoints: Explains what topology means in 3D
Covers quads and edge flow
Aimed at beginners

resources.title: Mesh Structure
resources.description: Official description of mesh elements, face types, normals, and topology concepts such as loops and poles.
keyPoints: A vertex is a single point in 3D space
Edges connect two vertices; faces form the rendered surface
Triangles, quads and n-gons; quads deform well
Edge and face loops matter for organic modeling and animation
Poles are vertices with 3, 5 or more edges

resources.title: UV Unwrapping for Beginners (Blender Tutorial)
resources.description: Beginner tutorial on unwrapping a model in Blender so textures apply cleanly.
keyPoints: Introduces UV unwrapping in Blender
Shows marking seams and unwrapping
Aimed at beginners

resources.title: UV Editor Introduction
resources.description: Explains what UVs are, the U and V directions, and why image-based texturing needs unwrapping.
keyPoints: UVs map 2D images onto 3D objects
U is the left-right and V the up-down direction of the flat map
Images give more control and realism than procedural textures for details
Unwrapping tells Blender how faces map to the image

resources.title: UV Unwrapping Operators
resources.description: Reference for Blender's unwrapping methods, including Unwrap along seams and Smart UV Project.
keyPoints: Unwrap flattens the mesh by cutting along seams
Smart UV Project cuts by an angle threshold
Smart UV Project suits mechanical objects and architecture
Angle Based and Conformal (LSCM) unwrap methods

stages.title: Rigging & Character Animation
stages.description: Building an armature, binding a mesh to it with weights, posing with FK and IK, and blocking a walk cycle.
learningObjectives: Explain what an armature and bones are and the role of Edit Mode vs Pose Mode
Bind a mesh to an armature and refine influence with weight painting
Compare forward and inverse kinematics
Name the key poses of a walk cycle

explainBack.question: Walk through rigging a simple character in Blender and making it walk: what the armature is, how the mesh follows it, when to use FK vs IK, and which key poses define the walk.
rubric: An armature is a skeleton-like object made of bones; Edit Mode shows its rest position and bones are posed and animated in Pose Mode
Ctrl-P > Armature Deform With Automatic Weights adds an Armature modifier and creates vertex groups named after bones, weighted by distance (bone heat); results often need manual fixes
Weight painting sets per-vertex influence from 0.0 (blue) to 1.0 (red)
FK poses bones in order from the root to the tip; IK lets you place the last bone of a chain and the rest of the chain rotates to follow
A walk cycle's key poses are contact, down (recoil), passing and up (high point), with arms swinging opposite to the legs

resources.title: Rigging for impatient people - Blender Tutorial
resources.description: A fast-paced overview of rigging a character in Blender.
keyPoints: Covers creating an armature
Shows binding a mesh to bones
Condensed for quick learning

resources.title: Armatures Introduction
resources.description: Explains armatures as skeletons of bones used for rigging, and how Edit Mode and Pose Mode differ.
keyPoints: An armature is like a real skeleton made of bones
A rig is the set of controls that moves a character, like puppet strings
Edit Mode always shows the rest position
Bone animation is done in Pose Mode, not Object Mode

resources.title: Armature Deform Parenting
resources.description: How to bind meshes to an armature with empty groups, automatic weights or envelope weights.
keyPoints: Select mesh, then armature, Ctrl-P > Armature Deform
Creates an Armature modifier
Automatic Weights uses a bone-heat algorithm based on distance
Vertex groups are named after the bones
Automatic results often need manual weight adjustment

resources.title: Weight Painting Introduction
resources.description: Explains weight painting vertex groups to control how strongly each bone deforms each vertex.
keyPoints: Weights range from 0 to 1 per vertex
Blue means near 0.0, red means near 1.0
The Armature modifier normalizes deforming weights
Also used for particles, modifiers and shape keys

resources.title: Inverse Kinematics Introduction
resources.description: Contrasts posing bone-by-bone from the root (FK) with IK, where moving the end of a chain positions the rest.
keyPoints: Normal posing sets bones from root to tip in sequence
IK positions the last bone; other bones follow automatically
Chain length 0 follows parent connections without limit
Auto IK rotates parents to follow a translated bone

resources.title: Animation walk cycle
resources.description: Overview of the four key poses of a walk cycle, arm swing and ways to add character.
keyPoints: Key poses: contact, recoil (down), passing, high point (up)
Contact: leading foot hits heel-first
Arms swing opposite to the legs
Posture and stride length convey personality

stages.title: Materials, Lighting & Rendering
stages.description: PBR materials with the Principled BSDF, three-point lighting, and choosing and tuning Blender's Eevee and Cycles render engines.
learningObjectives: Set up a PBR material using base color, metallic and roughness
Place key, fill and back lights for a three-point setup
Compare Eevee and Cycles
Explain how samples, noise and denoising trade off against render time

explainBack.question: You need a convincing render of a metal robot on a table. Describe how you would set up its materials, light it, choose a render engine and get a clean image.
rubric: The Principled BSDF is a physically based 'uber' shader: Metallic 0 is a dielectric, 1 is a metal; Roughness 0 is mirror-like, 1 fully diffuse
Three-point lighting: the key light is the main source, the fill (weaker than the key) softens its shadows, and the back light separates the subject from the background
Cycles is a path-tracing engine and gives more physically accurate results; Eevee is a real-time engine built for speed; both use the same shader nodes
In Cycles more samples reduce noise but take longer; adaptive sampling's noise threshold and denoisers (e.g. OpenImageDenoise, OptiX) clean the image

resources.title: PBR Materials: The Ultimate Guide (Blender Tutorial)
resources.description: A guide to building physically based materials in Blender.
keyPoints: Explains PBR materials in Blender
Covers Principled BSDF inputs
Shows texture map usage

resources.title: Principled BSDF
resources.description: Reference for Blender's physically based uber shader and its main inputs.
keyPoints: Based on Disney's principled model; compatible with other PBR software
Metallic: 0 dielectric, 1 metal
Roughness: 0 mirror-like, 1 fully diffuse
Specular for dielectrics is typically 0-8% reflectivity

resources.title: Blender Tutorial - 3 Point Lighting
resources.description: Demonstrates setting up three-point lighting in Blender.
keyPoints: Places key, fill and back lights in Blender
Shows the effect of each light
Short tutorial

resources.title: Three Point Lighting: Learn How to Use the Key, Fill, and Back Lights
resources.description: Explains the roles and placement of the key, fill and back lights; the same logic transfers to virtual lights.
keyPoints: Key light is the main source, often about 45 degrees to the side and above
Fill reduces key shadows and must be weaker than the key
Fill should not create a second shadow
Back light behind the subject creates a rim that separates it

resources.title: Eevee Introduction
resources.description: Describes Eevee as Blender's real-time PBR engine and contrasts it with path-traced Cycles.
keyPoints: Eevee is a real-time engine focused on speed and interactivity
Uses the same shader nodes as Cycles
Uses rasterization rather than tracing every light ray
Cycles gives more physically accurate renders

resources.title: Cycles Sampling
resources.description: Explains path-traced samples, noise, adaptive sampling and denoising options in Cycles.
keyPoints: Rays are traced from the camera until they reach light
More samples give less noise but longer renders
Noise threshold targets a noise level (typical 0.1-0.001)
Denoisers include OpenImageDenoise and OptiX

stages.title: Compositing & VFX Basics
stages.description: Combining layers with alpha and masks, pulling green-screen keys, rotoscoping, and tracking camera motion to place CG into footage.
learningObjectives: Explain the alpha channel and how masks and mattes control transparency
Pull a chroma key and clean it with garbage mattes and spill suppression
Explain rotoscoping and how tools propagate a matte across frames
Explain what 2D tracking and camera solving provide for compositing

explainBack.question: An actor was filmed on green screen with a moving camera, and you must put them into a CG set. Describe how you would separate them, handle problem areas, and match the camera.
rubric: The alpha channel is the fourth (A) channel of an RGBA image: white is opaque, black is transparent, grey is partly transparent
Chroma keying makes pixels close to a chosen colour (green/blue screen) transparent; a garbage matte roughly masks out areas, and spill suppression removes key colour from edges
Rotoscoping isolates a foreground object frame by frame; tools like Roto Brush propagate a matte from a base frame and need corrective strokes
Motion tracking follows features in footage; camera solving reconstructs the camera's 3D motion so CG objects can be matched to the shot

resources.title: Learn Green Screen VFX in Blender in UNDER 7 MINUTES
resources.description: A quick demonstration of keying green-screen footage and compositing it in Blender.
keyPoints: Keys green-screen footage in Blender
Composites the subject over a new background
Under seven minutes

resources.title: Alpha channels, masks, and mattes
resources.description: Explains alpha channels, masks, mask modes and feathering in compositing.
keyPoints: Alpha is the fourth (A) channel of an RGBA image
White = opaque, black = transparent, grey = partial
Masks are paths that modify a layer's alpha
Mask modes include Add, Subtract and Intersect; feathering softens edges

resources.title: Keying
resources.description: Covers colour, luminance and difference keying, Keylight, garbage mattes and spill suppression.
keyPoints: Keying makes pixels similar to a chosen value transparent
Colour keying is also called green/blue screening
Garbage mattes reduce keying work
Spill suppression removes key colour from edges
Use the least-compressed footage possible

resources.title: Roto Brush and Refine Matte
resources.description: Explains rotoscoping and how Roto Brush propagates a foreground matte across frames.
keyPoints: Rotoscoping separates foreground objects from the background
Paint foreground and background strokes on a base frame
The matte is propagated to later frames
Correct problem frames and refine edges like hair

resources.title: Camera Tracking in Blender for Beginners | Motion Tracking Tutorial
resources.description: Beginner tutorial on tracking footage and solving the camera in Blender.
keyPoints: Tracks features in live footage
Solves the camera motion in Blender
Places 3D objects into the shot

resources.title: Motion Tracking Introduction
resources.description: Overview of Blender's 2D tracking, camera and object solving, plane tracks and stabilization.
keyPoints: Tracks the motion of objects or a camera and applies it to 3D objects
Supports 2D tracking and 3D camera/object reconstruction
Plane tracks support compositing onto flat surfaces
Includes 2D stabilization for hand-held shake

stages.title: Render Passes, Color Management & Delivery
stages.description: Splitting renders into passes, rendering safe image sequences, managing scene-linear color with view transforms, and picking codecs for delivery.
learningObjectives: Explain render passes and how they are used in compositing
Explain why animations are rendered to image sequences before encoding
Describe scene-linear rendering and view transforms (Standard, Filmic, AgX)
Compare intra-frame and long-GOP codecs for editing vs delivery

explainBack.question: Plan the output of a 3D animated shot from render to final file: what you render, in which formats, how color is handled, and what you deliver.
rubric: Render passes split the image into components (e.g. diffuse, glossy, emission, AO) and data (depth/Z, normal, mist, Cryptomatte) so they can be adjusted in compositing without re-rendering
Render animations to image sequences (PNG or OpenEXR, which keeps HDR data) rather than straight to video, so a crash doesn't ruin the file and encoding can be redone without re-rendering

Rendering is done in scene-linear color; the view transform maps it to the display: Standard does no extra conversion, Filmic and AgX are tone-mapping transforms for high dynamic range (AgX improves on Filmic)
Intra-frame codecs (e.g. ProRes) store every frame fully and edit smoothly; long-GOP codecs (e.g. H.264) store changes between frames for much smaller files, suited to delivery

resources.title: Blender 2.9 for Production - 04 Render Layers, Light Passes & Data Passes
resources.description: Production-focused lesson on view/render layers and Blender's light and data passes.
keyPoints: Explains render (view) layers
Covers light passes such as diffuse and glossy
Covers data passes such as depth and normal

resources.title: Render Passes
resources.description: Lists Blender's render passes and explains how they split lighting and data for compositing.
keyPoints: Passes split images into colours and direct/indirect light
Data passes include Z depth, normal and mist (0-1)
Light passes include diffuse, glossy, AO and emission
Cryptomatte isolates objects in post

resources.title: Output Properties
resources.description: Explains output paths, frame-number padding, file formats and why to render animations as still-image sequences first.
keyPoints: Frame numbers are appended with zero padding (e.g. image0001.png)
Rendering straight to video is not recommended in the first instance
A crash can leave a video unplayable, forcing a full re-render
Render to PNG or OpenEXR (keeps HDR), then encode

resources.title: Color Management
resources.description: Explains display devices, scene-linear rendering, view transforms, looks, exposure and gamma.
keyPoints: Rendering uses scene-linear values: double the light, double the value
Standard view transform does no extra conversion
Filmic is a tone-mapping transform for high dynamic range
AgX improves on Filmic for more photorealistic results
Exposure (in stops) is applied before color space conversion

resources.title: A Primer: I-frame vs. GOP Video Compression
resources.description: Explains how intra-frame codecs like ProRes differ from GOP codecs like H.264 in file size, editing and quality.
keyPoints: I-frame codecs (ProRes) encode every frame completely
GOP codecs (H.264) store changes between frames
GOP files are far smaller, especially for static shots
I-frame media edits and scrubs more smoothly
GOP for efficient delivery; I-frame for editing and archiving

name: Animation & VFX
description: Learn animation and visual effects from the 12 principles and timing through keyframes, 3D modeling, rigging, rendering, compositing and final delivery, using free Blender as the default tool.
